blocks.text: TETRARCH OF ITURAEA AND TRACHONITIS, UNDER ROME · NEW TESTAMENT
Philip the tetrarch. Named once, in Luke's dating of John's preaching.
Not given c. 4 BC – AD 34 (dates vary)
“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", when John began to preach, Philip, Herod's brother…”
ROME: 17 RULERS HEROD THE GREAT → PORCIUS FESTUS
"In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar", when John began to preach, Philip, Herod's brother, was "tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis". Luke 3:1–3
From the textThis is the only verse that names him. Scripture records no word or deed of his, and no meeting with Jesus. Luke 3:1
Rome. Only places Scripture names are shown, each where the Atlas puts it.

Scholars' viewSchürer (1890) reports that Philip's coins carry the heads of Augustus and Tiberius and a temple, which he takes to be Herod's temple of Augustus at Paneas, the first likeness of an emperor on the coins of a Jewish prince; he explains it by a population mainly not Jewish.[9]
None. Luke names him in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1).
Tetrarch from 4 BC; died in the winter of AD 33/34, in the twentieth year of Tiberius.
Schürer (1890) reckons Luke's fifteenth year as running from August AD 28 to August AD 29, and so dates John's first preaching then. Luke 3:1 [15]
Counted from the year when Tiberius first shared authority over the provinces with Augustus; Ramsay finds Luke's statements of time then consistent. Luke 3:1 [35]
Only Luke 3:1 names him; Scripture records no word or deed of his.
Scripture does not say that Philip built Caesarea Philippi.
The "Philip" whose wife Herodias had been (Mark 6:17) is, on most views, a different man.
Scripture does not say whether its Bethsaida is the town Philip renamed Julias.
Luke names "his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis", the brother of Herod the tetrarch of Galilee. Luke 3:1
